_about: Living history seed for Church Street, Burlington, Vermont (Main St to Pearl St, the Marketplace blocks, the corners, and notable addresses just past Pearl and below Main). One record per building or address range, corner, or block, with a dated timeline of what was there. Every timeline entry has a source_url and a verified date: the date its claim was checked against that source. Entries marked via out-loud/stories.json were taken from the fact-checked Out Loud scripts and carry that pin's fact-check date. Entries from UVM HP206 student research pages carry an evidence field with a short verbatim excerpt. edition_url points to the Btown Brief edition that reported the item. numbers lists the individual street numbers a building record covers, so the app can look up 42 Church inside the 38-44 Church record. Historic street numbers changed around 1885 (HP206 notes 104-106 was 154 before 1885), so old addresses in evidence text may not match today's numbers. lat and lng are filled only where out-loud/stories.json recorded a reliable coordinate. Reader memories are meant to layer on later, keyed by id.

source_conflicts.issue: Lightning that took the original Unitarian steeple: Out Loud pin says 1954; HP206 Henderson cites an August 17, 1955 strike, removal in 1956 and replica in 1958.
Ethan Allen firehouse built 1887 (Marketplace tour, Out Loud) or 1889 (HP206 King, Champlain College library blog, Wikipedia). National Register listing 1971 (Out Loud) or 1970 (HP206 King).

Masonic Temple purchase for renovation: 1983 by Paul, Frank and Collins (Marketplace tour) or 1984 by the One Church Street Partnership (HP206 Henderson). Address given as 5 Church (tour), 1 Church (OSM via Out Loud) and 1-5 Church (Wikipedia via Out Loud). Meetings ended by 1970 (HP206) versus last Burlington lodge leaving in 2016 (Out Loud via Wikipedia).

Woolworth's building given as 37-42 Church (Marketplace tour) versus 37-45 and 37-39 (HP206 Cava); 1964 building called modernist with Googie elements (tour) versus Art Deco (HP206); largest of all Woolworth stores (tour) versus one of the largest in New England (HP206).
Warner Block range 90-98 (Marketplace tour) versus 90-96 (HP206 Telesca, with 98-100 as the Isham Block). Mrs. Wheeler's uncle named Charles Wheeler (tour) or Charles F. Warner (HP206).
Dear Lucy's final address: 38 Church in a Btown Brief listing (2026-01-09) and in HP206 (2018) versus 50 Church Street in Seven Days (2026-02-08).
Spelling Abernathy (Marketplace tour) versus Abernethy (Out Loud, most sources).

HP206 Tolstoi places the Sherwood hotel site at Church and Cherry and HP206 Cava calls the Woolworth lot the northwest corner of Cherry and Church; both cannot be the same corner. Records say only 'at Church and Cherry'.

City Hall Park survey form lists a 1931 Merchants Bank (#9) while HP206 King identifies 123 Church as the 1931 Chittenden County Trust Company building; survey numbers are not tied to street numbers in the form.

Subagent extraction flagged internal inconsistencies in the student pages, kept as written: 14-16 Church built 1872 and 1873; 10 Church built 1877 yet on the 1869 map; 98-100 a hardware store by 1885 but built 1894; post office completed 1857 but captioned 1855; Huntington's tenure 1837 or 1839; Strong's sale to the YMCA 1876 or 1886; first Court House 1795 or 1797; Town-City Hall 1853 or 1854; Opera House roof removed 1904 or 1905; 56-58 and 60-78 Church rebuilt 1974 or 1976.

timeline.detail: The Concert Hall Building stood on the southeast corner of Church and Cherry at least as early as 1830, based on the 1830 and 1853 maps.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: it was standing as least as early as 1830, based on comparisons of the 1830 Ammi B. Young map and the 1853 Presdee & Edwards map.

timeline.detail: An 1860 ad placed the Burlington Sentinel office on Concert Hall's ground floor, between two stores.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: an 1860 ad for the Burlington Sentinel describes their office as “on the ground floor of Concert Hall, between the stores of C.F. Staniford and C.W. Wingate.”

timeline.detail: A February 1863 ad placed H.M. Phelps' marble works in the Concert Hall building under the Times office. The 1862 Wainwright map also shows the marble works here.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: a February 1863 ad for H.M. Phelps’ marble works, which listed his business as “in Concert Hall building under the Times Office.”

timeline.detail: Soon after, Concert Hall burned or was demolished. Gunsmith Edward H. Payn built a three-story Italianate block. Masonry was nearly done by December 1863 and the interior near finished in April 1864.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: By December of the same year, the masonry work was nearly finished, and workers had begun removing the scaffolding.

timeline.detail: An April 1864 notice said the interior would soon be finished.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: Four months later, in April of 1864, another notice announced that the interior would soon be finished.

timeline.detail: The Free Press reported on August 19, 1864 that local Democrats rented a room in Payn's Block for weekly meetings.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: On August 19th, 1864, the Press noted that “the local Democrats have organized recently, whether as “Knights of the Golden Circle,” “American Knights,” or under some other title, we are not informed. They have rented a room in Payn’s Block

timeline.what: E.H. Payn's gun and engraving shop
timeline.detail: Payn expanded his business, adding engraving, locksmithing and stenciling in 1867, three employees by 1869, and two branch locations in 1879.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: In 1867, he changed his title from that of simply gunsmith to include engraving, locksmithing, and stenciling.

timeline.detail: An independent commercial college, founded in 1878, occupied the building until 1887.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: the Commercial College, which was founded in 1878 and left the building the same year as Payn.

timeline.detail: Payn sold his space at 38 Church in 1887 to the American Clothing Company's Red 46 Department Store, which grew to own all of Payn's Block and half of Nelson's Block. It closed in the late 1920s.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: In 1887, Payn consolidated his various offices and sold his space at 38 Church Street to the American Clothing Company’s Red 46 Department Store, managed by Robert and Mrs. F. Levin.

timeline.detail: Red 46 built a rear addition in 1910 that nearly doubled the first floor's length.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: The first was in 1910, when they built a major rear addition that nearly doubled the length of the first floor.

timeline.detail: In 1917 the upper floors were gutted and rearranged into show rooms.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: The second came in 1917, when the upper floors were gutted and rearranged to create better show rooms.

timeline.detail: The pressed metal facade uniting Payn's and Nelson's Blocks was added c. 1925.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: the current pressed metal facade was added to both Payn’s and Nelson’s Blocks circa 1925 to unite the two buildings.

timeline.what: Black Cap Coffee and Bakery at 42
timeline.detail: Black Cap's Burlington location at 42 Church Street closed at the end of 2025 amid a strike; owner Laura Vilalta cited two years of declining sales and denied the union was a factor.
timeline.source_label: Seven Days, 2025-12-09

timeline.detail: HP206 lists Dear Lucy in Payn's Block as of 2018. Seven Days says Dear Lucy later combined with Whim in a larger storefront at 50 Church Street in spring 2025 and closed in January 2026.
timeline.source_label: Seven Days, 2026-02-08
timeline.note: A Btown Brief listing on 2026-01-09 put the Dear Lucy closing sale at 38 Church Street; Seven Days puts the final store at 50 Church Street.

timeline.detail: PopUp Bagels, founded in Connecticut, announced its first Vermont location at 42 Church St.; no opening date was given in May 2026.
As of 2018 Payn's Block housed Dear Lucy, Pokiworks and Uncommon Grounds.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: Today, Payn’s Block houses Dear Lucy, Pokiworks, and Uncommon Grounds.

timeline.detail: In 1862 furniture maker Henry J. Nelson and grocer Augustus Barrows owned neighboring buildings on the lot, each under a decade old.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: they owned neighboring buildings on the lot in 1862, which themselves were less than a decade old

timeline.detail: The three-story Italianate block was likely built in 1866, as it first appears in the 1867 directory.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: was likely built in 1866. There are few details concerning its construction, but as it is first mentioned in the 1867 city directory, it was likely finished soon before.

timeline.detail: Barrows was among the first businesses in 1867 and left by 1885, replaced by a dry goods store and others.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: Barrows’ business left the building by 1885 and was replaced by a dry goods store and others

timeline.detail: Nelson's business stayed until his death in April 1910. The building was then sold to the American Clothing Company.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: Nelson’s business, on the other hand, remained in the building up until his death in April of 1910, after which it was also sold to the American Clothing Company

timeline.detail: Red 46 Department Store expanded into the building in 1906.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: eventually leading to the Red 46 Department Store’s expansion into the space in 1906.

timeline.detail: The pressed metal facade shared with Payn's Block was added c. 1925.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: the current pressed metal facade was added to both Payn’s and Nelson’s Blocks circa 1925 to unite the two buildings.

timeline.detail: Melissa Desautels merged Whim into Dear Lucy at 50 Church Street in May 2025. Dear Lucy announced its Burlington closing in January 2026.
timeline.note: The 50 Church address comes from Seven Days, 2026-02-08 (Whim article).

timeline.detail: As of 2018 the block held the Catamount Store and Fjallraven Burlington.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: Today, Nelson’s Block is home to the Catamount Store and Fjällräven Burlington.

now.name: Burlington Square (former mall site; remaining mall stub and L.L. Bean building vacant)

timeline.what: Central House hotel, L. D. Turrill
timeline.detail: L. D. Turrill was proprietor of the Central House, advertised in the 1865 city directory.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: West Side between Cherry and Bank Streets, by Joseph Cava, 2018
timeline.evidence: In 1865, L. D. Turrill was the proprietor of the Central House.

timeline.detail: Colvin kept an office in his private residence at 49 Church Street in 1881.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: West Side between Cherry and Bank Streets, by Joseph Cava, 2018
timeline.evidence: H. E. Colvin, who was a homeopathic physician and surgeon, with an office he operated out of his private residence at 49 Church Street in 1881.

timeline.what: Central House demolished; Central House Block
timeline.detail: The 1885 Sanborn map shows the Central House demolished and replaced by a six bay Italianate building renamed the Central House Block.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: West Side between Cherry and Bank Streets, by Joseph Cava, 2018
timeline.evidence: The 1885 map showed that the Central House had been demolished and was replaced by a six bay Italianate style building (Figure 2) renamed the Central House Block.

timeline.detail: (Barrows Block) The 1894 Sanborn map shows the remaining lot space filled by the three bay masonry Barrows Block with elliptical windows and a spire. The page gives no street number.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: West Side between Cherry and Bank Streets, by Joseph Cava, 2018
timeline.evidence: The 1894 Sanborn is notable because the remaining lot space had been filled by the construction of the Barrows Block.

timeline.what: Central House Block demolished for Kresge
timeline.detail: The block was demolished for S. S. Kresge Company's new department store and renamed the Kresge Block.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: West Side between Cherry and Bank Streets, by Joseph Cava, 2018
timeline.evidence: In 1930 the Central House Block was demolished to make room for S. S. Kresge Company’s new department store.

timeline.detail: Kresge operated about 35 years before going out of business in 1965.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: West Side between Cherry and Bank Streets, by Joseph Cava, 2018
timeline.evidence: In 1965 when it went out of business it was replaced by the Jupiter department store.

timeline.detail: Jupiter replaced Kresge in 1965; its run ended when the Kresge Block was torn down in 1976.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: West Side between Cherry and Bank Streets, by Joseph Cava, 2018
timeline.evidence: Jupiter’s time on Church Street was short lived when the Kresge Block was torn down for the construction of the new suburban styled mall in 1976.

timeline.detail: The mall, designed by Alexander & Truex Architects, was Burlington's primary bicentennial project and part of an urban renewal zone; its open metal entrance was later enclosed in brick.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: West Side between Cherry and Bank Streets, by Joseph Cava, 2018
timeline.evidence: Nearly five decades ago the mall was constructed in the 1976 as part of an Urban Renewal zone in Burlington that leveled a 27-acre portion of the downtown.

timeline.detail: The indoor mall opened November 1, 1976 as the Burlington Square Mall with Porteous as anchor, later renamed Burlington Town Center. Filene's, later Macy's, came in 1999 and L.L. Bean in 2014.
timeline.source_label: Wikipedia, CityPlace Burlington
timeline.note: Wikipedia as cited in the fact-checked pin.

timeline.what: Mall built as a competitor to suburbs
timeline.detail: Bob Blanchard's stroll describes the 1976 mall as an attempt to compete with suburban shopping centers.
timeline.source_label: Seven Days, Stuck in Vermont: Strolling Through Church Street's Past With Bob Blanchard, 2026-06-25

timeline.what: Mall bought by Don Sinex for CityPlace
timeline.detail: Developer Don Sinex bought the mall for $25 million to build the 14 story, $225 million CityPlace Burlington.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: West Side between Cherry and Bank Streets, by Joseph Cava, 2018
timeline.evidence: In 2013 the mall was purchased for $25 million by developer, Don Sinex to construct a new tall building (Figure 5) capped off at 14 stories called CityPlace Burlington.

timeline.detail: An investor group bought the property in December 2013 for $25 million and in November 2014 proposed a $200 million rebuild.
timeline.source_label: Wikipedia, CityPlace Burlington

timeline.detail: Demolition began in December 2017, then work stopped for four years and the site became known as the pit. Local developers restarted construction in 2022.
timeline.source_label: Vermont Public, A decade later, Burlington's downtown mall redevelopment opens (Sept 25, 2025)

timeline.detail: Delays in August 2018 slowed construction; Sinex hoped to open retail and parking by early 2020 and finish by January 2021. As of 2018, 49 Church Street is the entrance to what remains of the mall.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: West Side between Cherry and Bank Streets, by Joseph Cava, 2018
timeline.evidence: Recent delays in August 2018 have delayed Sinex’s construction progress, but he hopes to have retail space and the parking garage open by early 2020

timeline.detail: Macy's, the only department store downtown, closed in March 2018; Burlington High School used the building from 2021 to 2026.
timeline.note: The Macy's building fronts Cherry Street behind the mall rather than Church Street.

timeline.detail: The AC Hotel by Marriott opened September 18, 2025 with apartments following; the first phase has 161 hotel rooms and 53 apartments.

In March 2026 the north tower was 90 percent enclosed and the project was aimed at late 2027 or early 2028. In October 2026 developers presented Phase 2, which would replace the rest of the former mall and the old L.L. Bean building with 314 apartments.
timeline.note: Phase 2 details are from the Btown Brief 2026-10-19 listing for the Ward 3 NPA meeting at 29 Church Street, linked to a Front Porch Forum calendar post, not independently fetched.

timeline.detail: After the 1929 fire Montgomery Ward bought half the lot and built a two-story store to a standard company design, opening December 28. It closed in 1961.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: the 1929 Montgomery Ward Building (#52-54) and a modern commercial building (#56-58).

timeline.detail: Montgomery Ward opened its 515th store here on December 28, 1929, with the terracotta Spirit of Progress figure on the parapet. It closed in 1961; later tenants included a bargain store, a furniture company and a bank. The building is separately listed on the National Register.
timeline.source_label: Church Street Marketplace and Preservation Burlington, Historic Tours page

timeline.detail: Since the 1961 closure the building has hosted a number of businesses.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: Since the department store’s closure in 1961, it has hosted a number of businesses.

timeline.detail: Homeport, the kitchen and gift store on the Marketplace, signed a lease for a second store at the Essex Experience in March 2026; the Burlington store stays open.
timeline.source_label: Seven Days, 2026-03-13
timeline.note: Homeport's address of 52 Church comes from HP206 (2018) and a Btown Brief listing (2026-05-08).

timeline.detail: As of 2018 it housed Designer's Circle and Homeport.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: Today, it is home to Designer’s Circle and Homeport.

photos.ref: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018, Fig. 7
photos.caption: The Montgomery Ward Building, viewed from the southwest. Credit: Photo taken by Chris Rizer in 2018

timeline.detail: The 1830 Ammi B. Young map shows the Chittenden County House, the County Jail and a barn on this lot.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: The first known buildings on this lot, as early as the 1830 Ammi B. Young map, were the Chittenden County House, where the county sheriff/jailor lived, County Jail, and an associated barn.

timeline.detail: The frame buildings were all destroyed by fire on January 29, 1851.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: they were all destroyed by fire on January 29th, 1851.

timeline.detail: A new brick County House and Jail and a new barn were completed by 1853. Between 1862 and 1869 the jail was remodeled and almost doubled.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: a new brick County House and Jail and replacement of the barn, both of which were completed by 1853.

timeline.detail: Poorly maintained, the jail stood until 1887, when the lot was sold for $12,000 to a company owned by Augustus Barrows, Lewis M. Barrows and H.L. Bundy.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: That buyer, at a price of $12,000, was a real estate corporation owned by Augustus Barrows, Lewis M. Barrows, and H.L. Bundy.

timeline.detail: Barrows and Bundy finished a four-story commercial block in April 1888 for about $30,000, with stores, tenements and a fourth-floor ballroom.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: Barrows and Bundy then put up a four-story commercial block at a cost of approximately $30,000, which was finished in April of 1888.

timeline.detail: The largest tenants were Miles and McMahon's Boots and Shoes and the Boston Store, filling most of the first two floors.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: Of the commercial interests in the building, by far the two largest were Miles and McMahon’s Boots & Shoes and the Boston Store, owned by M.J. Leo and P.F. McLaren.

timeline.detail: After Augustus Barrows died in 1897, the J.W. McAuslan Company bought the Boston Store and the building.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: until 1897, at which point Augustus Barrows died and the J.W. McAuslan Company bought the Boston Store and the rest of the building.

timeline.what: Fisher Bros, then Rutland Combination Cash Store
timeline.detail: The Boston Store was sold in 1908 to the Fisher Bros, who sold it to the Rutland Combination Cash Store. A tenement fire during their ownership was quickly put out.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: They continued operating the Boston Store until 1908, when it was sold to the Fisher Bros, who then sold it to the Rutland Combination Cash Store.

timeline.what: Green Brothers' Store, destroyed by fire
timeline.detail: The Green Brothers' Store ran the building until a 1929 fire destroyed it.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: The building was then sold to the Green Brothers’ Store, who operated it until a fire destroyed the building in 1929.

photos.caption: Circa 1890 view of Church Street showing the Barrows Block soon after its 1888 construction

timeline.detail: The 1974 fire that destroyed Stetson's Row also destroyed the southern half of the old jail and Barrows Block lot.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: This is the southern half of the Jail and Barrows Block Lot, which was destroyed along with Stetson's Row in the 1974 fire.

timeline.detail: A concrete block building with brick veneer was built in 1976. It housed Banana Republic as of 2018.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: The first, built in 1976, filled the other half of the Barrows lot as was previously mentioned, and currently houses Banana Republic.

timeline.detail: The three story Italianate Union Block first appears on the 1869 Sanborn map.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: West Side between Cherry and Bank Streets, by Joseph Cava, 2018
timeline.evidence: In the 1869 Sanborn Fire Insurance Map the Union Block, 57-59 Church Street, and the Central Block, 61-75 Church Street (Figure 6) first appeared

timeline.detail: Dressmaker Bertha Church first appears living on the second floor of 59 Church Street.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: West Side between Cherry and Bank Streets, by Joseph Cava, 2018
timeline.evidence: Bertha Church first appeared in 1940 when she lived on the second floor of 59 Church Street.

timeline.detail: As of 2018, Hatley is at 59 Church Street and Zinnia's at 57.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: West Side between Cherry and Bank Streets, by Joseph Cava, 2018
timeline.evidence: Hatley is located at 59 Church Street and Zinnia’s at 57 Church Street.

timeline.what: Shedd and Walkers, glass and tinware
timeline.detail: J. A. Shedd is listed in the Union Block in partnership with Walkers, a glass and tinware dealer; no year in the text.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: West Side between Cherry and Bank Streets, by Joseph Cava, 2018
timeline.evidence: Shedd is listed again in the Union Block in a business partnership with Walkers who was a dealer in glass and tinware.

timeline.detail: Demolished in the 1970s during the urban renewal project that produced the mall; two small ground floor shopfronts replaced it.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: West Side between Cherry and Bank Streets, by Joseph Cava, 2018
timeline.evidence: The fashionable, three story Union Block was demolished in the 1970s as part of the Urban Renewal project

photos.ref: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: West Side between Cherry and Bank Streets, by Joseph Cava, 2018, Fig. 7
photos.caption: October 2018 view of Burlington Town Center Mall and shops along Church Street looking northwest. Credit: Courtesy Joseph Cava

timeline.detail: In 1830 this was the most developed part of the block, with three brick buildings. A fourth store was added before 1851.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: In 1830, this was the most developed section of the block, known as Stetson’s Row or Stetson’s Block and home to three brick buildings.

timeline.detail: The January 1851 fire that destroyed the County Jail began in a cellar at the south end near Bank Street and destroyed the row. Twelve families lost their homes.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: A fourth store was added between then and 1851, but it was for naught, as the same fire that destroyed the County Jail destroyed Stetson’s Row as well.

timeline.detail: By 1869 the row was rebuilt and expanded as three frame buildings with six businesses.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: Yet, by 1869, the entire row had been rebuilt and expanded in the fashionable Italianate style. That year, the Row consisted of three frame buildings that housed six businesses.

timeline.what: W.W. Wood's Boots and Shoes and neighbors
timeline.detail: Tenants from 60 Church southward were W.W. Wood's Boots and Shoes, C. Storrs and Son's Market, David Valpee's shoemaking, a milliner, Henry A. Mooney's Boots and Shoes, and Moody Haskell's shop and home.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: Beginning at 60 Church Street and working south, they were W.W. Wood’s Boots & Shoes, C. Storrs and Son’s Market, David Valpee’s shoemaking, a milliner, Henry A. Mooney’s Boots & Shoes, and Moody Haskell’s shop and home.

timeline.detail: By 1889 W.W. Wood had rebuilt his store in brick with a third story, and the four southern businesses had been joined into one mass.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: Twenty years later, in 1889, expansion was still ongoing on Stetson’s Row. W.W. Wood had rebuilt his store in brick and added a third story.

timeline.detail: Mary Currier's Ladies Clothing Store at 66 Church was rebuilt in brick. Otherwise little changed until 1974.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: the rebuilding of Mary Currier’s Ladies Clothing Store at 66 Church Street in brick

timeline.detail: A 1974 fire destroyed all of Stetson's Row, roughly the same area as in 1851.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: That year, disaster struck yet again, and a fire destroyed essentially the same area that it had in 1851.

timeline.detail: A small two-story shopping center with four or so businesses was built in 1976.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks: Bank Street to Cherry Street, East Side, by Christopher Rizer, 2018
timeline.evidence: The other, built in the same year, is a small two-story shopping center that houses four or so businesses.

timeline.detail: Whim occupied the narrow space at 62 Church Street for about 18 years before merging into Dear Lucy in spring 2025.
timeline.source_label: Seven Days, 2026-02-08

timeline.detail: Ava Stanley moved her children's shop Olive and Ollie into the old Whim space in December 2025 before relaunching Whim there.
timeline.source_label: Seven Days, 2026-02-08

timeline.detail: Ava Stanley, Whim's manager from 2018 to 2021, planned to relaunch Whim at 62 Church Street in April 2026 under new ownership.
timeline.source_label: Seven Days, 2026-02-08

timeline.detail: Shlomi and Miriam Lavi own Flora and Fauna, a large second-floor curiosity and gift store at 70 Church Street.
timeline.source_label: Seven Days, 2026-06-29

timeline.detail: After the 1894 fire D.A. Brodie bought out M.L. Kelsey and rebuilt; Pease and Manson clothing took the first floor, Miller & Miller veterinary surgeons the second. D.W.C. Clapp ran the rebuilding.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Church Street East Side between College Street and Bank Street, by Andrew Telesca, 2018
timeline.evidence: Once complete, the first floor was occupied by the clothing store Pease and Manson.

photos.ref: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Church Street East Side between College Street and Bank Street, by Andrew Telesca, 2018, Fig. 7
photos.caption: West facade of 110 and 108 Church Street, built 1970 by Antonio Pomerleau on the Brodie Block site. Credit: Photograph by Andrew Telesca

timeline.detail: Rann's county history records no building on the corner in 1825.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Between Bank and College Streets, West Side, by Greg Socinski, 2018
timeline.evidence: as Rann indicates no structure was there in 1825.

timeline.what: Building shown on Ammi B. Young map
timeline.detail: The 1830 map shows a rectangular footprint similar to the present building.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Between Bank and College Streets, West Side, by Greg Socinski, 2018
timeline.evidence: Our earliest map, the 1830 Ammi Burnham Young map, shows a similar rectangular footprint to the one currently occupied by the Leunig’s Building

timeline.what: Abraham's Block and Sherman Block facades
timeline.detail: The Marketplace tour dates the joined blocks to 1830 and 1847, with Art Deco and Streamline Moderne facade work by Lewis Newton in 1933 and 1946 and Roland Whittier in 1956.
timeline.source_label: Church Street Marketplace and Preservation Burlington, Historic Tours page

timeline.detail: Hagar had been in business on the corner since 1836; 'Hagar & Arthur' advertised hardware, drugs and paints by 1848. I.M. Hagar later traded at 174 College St.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Between Bank and College Streets, West Side, by Greg Socinski, 2018
timeline.evidence: Hagar had been in business there since 1836.

timeline.what: Present building constructed under shared-ownership contract
timeline.detail: Owners agreed to build one Federal-style structure shared between them; the split ownership explains the divided east facade. The page calls this the building that stands today, greatly altered.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Between Bank and College Streets, West Side, by Greg Socinski, 2018
timeline.evidence: in 1847 the owners entered into an unusual contract where a new building would be constructed with both owners sharing ownership in this single structure.

timeline.what: Divided storefronts shown on Sanborn map
timeline.detail: The 1869 Sanborn map shows storefronts numbered 115 and 113 on Church St and a separate business at 174 College St.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Between Bank and College Streets, West Side, by Greg Socinski, 2018
timeline.evidence: Our earliest Sanborn Fire Insurance map of 1869 reflects this as the original delineation of the building as the storefronts on Church Street, numbered 115 and 113, seem to follow the façade’s division.

timeline.what: Central Drug Store at 115 Church St
timeline.detail: Tobacco and drug store that opened June 1875 on the corner and lasted, under changing names and owners, until after a 1929 fire; it closed the following year after over fifty years.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Between Bank and College Streets, West Side, by Greg Socinski, 2018
timeline.evidence: it was occupied by the Central Drug Store, which opened in June 1875, at the “corner of Church and College Sts”

timeline.what: Morris Abraham opens cigar store at 113 Church St
timeline.detail: Morris Abraham opened a cigar and tobacco store at 113 Church St, making cigars on the upper floors.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Between Bank and College Streets, West Side, by Greg Socinski, 2018
timeline.evidence: before coming to Burlington to open up a store in 1889.

timeline.what: Abraham's Cut-Rate Drug Store; 'Patent Medicine War'
timeline.detail: Abraham added drugs in 1899, angering other druggists; the Burlington Free Press reported a 'Patent Medicine War'.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Between Bank and College Streets, West Side, by Greg Socinski, 2018
timeline.evidence: in 1899, he bills his business as “Abraham’s Cut-Rate Drug Store.”

timeline.what: Bijou Tobacco Store at 115 Church St
timeline.detail: A competing tobacco store opened on the corner three months after the dispute.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Between Bank and College Streets, West Side, by Greg Socinski, 2018
timeline.evidence: After the great “Patent Medicine War of 1899,” The Bijou Tobacco Store took up residence on this corner

timeline.what: Hagar Hardware leaves for 98 Church St
timeline.detail: Hagar opened a second store at 98 Church St in the early 1920s and moved there entirely in 1923.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Between Bank and College Streets, West Side, by Greg Socinski, 2018
timeline.evidence: In the early 1920’s Hagar Hardware and Paint Company opened up another story nearby at 98 Church Street before moving there entirely in 1923.

timeline.detail: A Christmas Eve 1929 fire caused about $20,000 in damage to the store's interior and stock.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Between Bank and College Streets, West Side, by Greg Socinski, 2018
timeline.evidence: the Central Drug Store would endure here until Christmas Eve 1929, when a fire broke out, extensively damaging interior and stock of the business to the tune of $20,000.

timeline.what: W.E. Peters florist shop (174 College St section)
timeline.detail: A few years after Hagar left, W.E. Peters bought this section for his florist shop. In late 1932 the building was put up for forced sale and bought by the Chittenden County Trust Company. The page also gives Peters' new address as 128 Church.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Between Bank and College Streets, West Side, by Greg Socinski, 2018
timeline.evidence: In late 1932, his brick building and all his business’s contents were put up for a forced sale

timeline.what: Hyman Abraham buys 174 College St section; Art Deco storefront
timeline.detail: The bank sold the space to Hyman Abraham in July 1933, starting his real estate business. Architect Louis S. Newton designed an Art Deco storefront of black carrara glass for 111 Church St (dated 1933 in Fig. 4 caption).
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Between Bank and College Streets, West Side, by Greg Socinski, 2018
timeline.evidence: subsequent sale in July 1933 to Hyman Abraham would make it possible.

timeline.detail: Abraham doubled his store into the 174 College space; Newton encased that part in cream-and-brown enameled sheet metal with glass-block windows and an 'ABRAHAM'S' parapet. Year from Fig. 4 caption.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Between Bank and College Streets, West Side, by Greg Socinski, 2018
timeline.evidence: Here we see Hyman Abraham's 1946 alterations of the building, creating a disinctive double facade.

timeline.what: A. Schulte cigar store at 115 Church St
timeline.detail: A New York regional chain moved in shortly after Abraham's 1933 purchase and stayed over twenty years.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Between Bank and College Streets, West Side, by Greg Socinski, 2018
timeline.evidence: It would remain here for over twenty years, when in 1954 it closed and re-opened under local ownership as “Schulte’s of Vermont”.

timeline.detail: Locally owned successor to A. Schulte; its owners declared bankruptcy and closed in 1958.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Between Bank and College Streets, West Side, by Greg Socinski, 2018
timeline.evidence: even after Schulte’s of Vermont owners declared bankruptcy and closed shop in 1958.

timeline.what: Abraham buys final section; whole building sheathed
timeline.detail: Abraham bought the corner section in July 1955 and extended the modern facade over the entire exterior.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Between Bank and College Streets, West Side, by Greg Socinski, 2018
timeline.evidence: was able to purchase this section of the building in July 1955.

timeline.what: Irwin Abrams takes over after Hyman Abraham's death
timeline.detail: Abrams phased out the pharmacy by the 1980s and focused on photography.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Between Bank and College Streets, West Side, by Greg Socinski, 2018
timeline.evidence: After Hyman’s death in 1974, Irwin Abrams would take over ownership of the business and phase out the pharmacy by the 80s, dedicating the business full time to photography.

timeline.detail: Leunig's opened in 1980 and gradually expanded through the building, adding a College St porch in the 1990s and a second-floor lounge.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Between Bank and College Streets, West Side, by Greg Socinski, 2018
timeline.evidence: They first opened in 1980 and have been there since

timeline.what: Leunig's described as a fixture since 1980
timeline.detail: Btown Brief's restaurant review calls Leunig's Bistro and Cafe a fixture on Church Street since 1980.
timeline.source_label: Btown Brief restaurant review, 2025-07-14

timeline.detail: Abrams' son and an associate set up an advertising photography business in the building.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Between Bank and College Streets, West Side, by Greg Socinski, 2018
timeline.evidence: His son and an associate even set up a professional advertising photography business in the building in 1982.

timeline.detail: Abraham's closed on Christmas Eve 2003, after 115 years overall.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Between Bank and College Streets, West Side, by Greg Socinski, 2018
timeline.evidence: who finally closed on Christmas Eve 2003, after Irwin’s 45 years in the camera business here and Abraham’s 115 years overall.

timeline.detail: Leunig's got approval to replace the 'Abraham's' parapet letters; vinyl panels cover the older lettering.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Between Bank and College Streets, West Side, by Greg Socinski, 2018
timeline.evidence: in 2006 they got approval to change the letters reading “Abraham’s” along the building’s parapet to read “Leunig’s”

timeline.detail: Leunig's Bistro & Cafe at 115 Church St and Danforth Pewter at 111 Church St.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Between Bank and College Streets, West Side, by Greg Socinski, 2018
timeline.evidence: Today Leunig’s Bistro & Café is located at 115 Church Street and Danforth Pewter further north at 111 Church Street.

timeline.detail: Morris's nephew Hyman Abraham came to Burlington after his uncle's death and was proprietor by the early 1920s.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Between Bank and College Streets, West Side, by Greg Socinski, 2018
timeline.evidence: by the early 1920s he was the proprietor.

timeline.what: A&W on the corner; Abraham's Camera Center begins
timeline.detail: In the 1960s A&W replaced the long-running tobacco and drug store on the corner, and Irwin Abrams started Abraham's Camera Center above the drug store.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Church Street Between Bank and College Streets, West Side, by Greg Socinski, 2018
timeline.evidence: The 1960s finally put an end to the long-running tobacco and drug store on the corner when A&W, a long-running root beer and burger chain, moved into this location.

story_hooks: Did you fill a prescription or buy film at Abraham's?

timeline.detail: The 1860s photo shows a narrow two-story Italianate building, but the 1869 Sanborn map shows a three-story gable roofed structure.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Church Street East Side between College Street and Bank Street, by Andrew Telesca, 2018
timeline.evidence: However, the 1869 Sanborn map shows a three-story structure here with a gable roof.

timeline.detail: Myer Lippa started the business in 1933. It occupied two other spots on the street before settling at 112 Church Street, and in June 2026 announced a move to an appointment-only showroom in Colchester after 93 years.
timeline.source_label: Seven Days, 2026-06-23

timeline.detail: The grocery operated here for forty-one years before the 1947 fire forced it to relocate to South Burlington.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Church Street East Side between College Street and Bank Street, by Andrew Telesca, 2018
timeline.evidence: A. Verret and Sons’ Grocery, who had operated from this location for forty-one years, were forced to relocate to a newly reconstructed store in South Burlington.

timeline.detail: On June 19, 1947, a malfunctioning electric motor started a fire that destroyed the building.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Church Street East Side between College Street and Bank Street, by Andrew Telesca, 2018
timeline.evidence: On June 19th, 1947, a malfunctioning electric motor started a fire, which destroyed the building.

timeline.detail: Wrecking crews razed the building on July 9, 1947, with tow-trucks pulling down the walls.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Church Street East Side between College Street and Bank Street, by Andrew Telesca, 2018
timeline.evidence: On July 9th, 1947, wrecking crews razed the building, as tow-trucks pulled the walls down in a dramatic spectacle.

timeline.detail: A later two-story mid-century building stands on the site (no year given); as of 2018 Lippa Jewelers occupies it.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Church Street East Side between College Street and Bank Street, by Andrew Telesca, 2018
timeline.evidence: A later “mid century,” two-story building was later constructed on the site, and still stands today. This space is currently occupied by Lippa Jewelers.

photos.ref: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Church Street East Side between College Street and Bank Street, by Andrew Telesca, 2018, Fig. 6
photos.caption: West facade of 112 Church Street, built after the Verret grocery was demolished. Credit: Photograph by Andrew Telesca

timeline.detail: A three-and-a-half story Federal brick building seen in the early 1860s photo is potentially the L-shaped structure on Young's 1830 plan.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Church Street East Side between College Street and Bank Street, by Andrew Telesca, 2018
timeline.evidence: This is potentially the large L-shaped structure which occupies the space in Ammi Burnham Young’s 1830 Plan of Burlington Village.

timeline.detail: A new three-and-a-half story brick bank building, likely Romanesque Revival, was built for the First National Bank.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Church Street East Side between College Street and Bank Street, by Andrew Telesca, 2018
timeline.evidence: In 1867, a new three-and-a-half story brick building was built for the First National Bank in 1867.

timeline.detail: The 1867 building was taken down and replaced with a three-story granite faced building for the new Howard Bank.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Church Street East Side between College Street and Bank Street, by Andrew Telesca, 2018
timeline.evidence: In 1902, this building was taken down, and replaced with yet another three-story, granite faced building for the new Howard Bank.

timeline.detail: The 1862 map caption says Herrick appears to have owned the 114 property until his estate sold it in 1905; he may have built a three-story structure there around 1867.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Church Street East Side between College Street and Bank Street, by Andrew Telesca, 2018
timeline.evidence: Herrick appears to have owned the property up until 1905, when his estate sold it to the Chittenden County Trust Company.

timeline.what: 114 sold for Chittenden County Trust Company
timeline.detail: The Herrick estate sold the store to create a new banking house for the Chittenden County Trust Company.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Church Street East Side between College Street and Bank Street, by Andrew Telesca, 2018
timeline.evidence: Ultimately in 1905, the estate of S.L. Herrick sold the store with the intentions of creating a new banking house for the Chittenden County Trust Company.

timeline.detail: After Beeman's lease expired April 1, 1906, architect W.R. Wilcox gave the store a new front facade and interior.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Church Street East Side between College Street and Bank Street, by Andrew Telesca, 2018
timeline.evidence: Upon the expiration lease on April 1st, 1906, Mr. Beeman’s store would be extensively renovated, with a new front façade and transformed interior.

timeline.detail: The bank doubled its width northward; the 114 building was bought, torn down, and rebuilt as part of the bank, by Thomas M. James Company of Boston.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Church Street East Side between College Street and Bank Street, by Andrew Telesca, 2018
timeline.evidence: In 1942, Howard National Bank expanded to the north, doubling the width of the existing building.

timeline.detail: As of 2018 the salon occupies the first and second floors of the bank building and its expansion.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Church Street East Side between College Street and Bank Street, by Andrew Telesca, 2018
timeline.evidence: Stephen & Burns, an Aveda salon, currently occupies the first and second floors of the Howard Bank Building and its subsequent expansion into the space next door.

timeline.detail: The three-story Italianate building at 114 housed Beeman's dry goods, cloaks, and suits store; the Fig. 18 postcard dates it to c. 1903 or 1904.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Church Street East Side between College Street and Bank Street, by Andrew Telesca, 2018
timeline.evidence: B.B. Beeman & Co. continued the tradition of selling dry goods, cloaks, and suits from this location.

timeline.detail: The state survey form describes the McAuliffe Building, built in 1928, as having a Style Moderne facade of patterned brickwork; it is one of the buildings seen looking west from Church Street.
timeline.source_label: Vermont Division for Historic Preservation, City Hall Park Historic District survey form (John Page, 2010)

timeline.detail: Rebuilt after the 1928 fire on the former Huntington section; reuses the YMCA Block's red sandstone ground floor. Three-story brick office building built by James Cashman.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, The City Hall Block - College Street to Main Street, West Side, by Adam King, 2018
timeline.evidence: was rebuilt by the MacAuliffe Paper Company to become known as what is now 117 Church Street.

timeline.detail: Carved names and dates mark Huntington (1837 to 1888) and McAuliffe (1912 to the 1928 fire). Stained glass advertising books and stationery survives, obscured by awnings.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, The City Hall Block - College Street to Main Street, West Side, by Adam King, 2018
timeline.evidence: 1837 to 1888 are the dates during which Samuel Huntington's businesses occupied that corner prior to the construction of the YMCA Block

photos.ref: UVM HP206, The City Hall Block - College Street to Main Street, West Side, by Adam King, 2018, Figure 18
photos.caption: Extant corner of the former YMCA block today

timeline.what: Building on corner since at least 1830
timeline.detail: A three-story side-gabled masonry building stood here for decades with a clothing store on the first floor.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Main to College: A History of the East Side, by Samantha Johnson, 2018
timeline.evidence: it is no surprise that a building has occupied the site since at least 1830.

timeline.what: Clothing stores and upstairs photography studio
timeline.detail: Clothing stores under various proprietors until the 1910s, including Stiles & Kelley; a photography studio ran until 1925 and a dentist rented space.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Main to College: A History of the East Side, by Samantha Johnson, 2018
timeline.evidence: These photographs and directories document the presence of a clothing store at this address operated by different proprietors until the 1910s.

timeline.what: Paul D. Kelley grocery; building demolished
timeline.detail: Kelley's grocery briefly used the first floor before demolition in 1925.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Main to College: A History of the East Side, by Samantha Johnson, 2018
timeline.evidence: Prior to its demolition in 1925, the first floor operated briefly as Paul D. Kelley’s grocery store.

timeline.detail: Colonial Revival bank by James W. O'Connor, commissioned 1925, with Vermont marble, brick and slate. Plaque reads 'Burlington Trust Co. 1882-1826' (sic).
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Main to College: A History of the East Side, by Samantha Johnson, 2018
timeline.evidence: this building was replaced with a beautiful, high-style Colonial Revival structure in 1926

timeline.detail: The trust merged with Howard National Bank in 1952 and sold the building.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Main to College: A History of the East Side, by Samantha Johnson, 2018
timeline.evidence: In that year, the building was sold to Miles & Riley, proprietors of a men’s clothing store that operated until 1969

timeline.detail: Novelty woodworking retail outlet.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Main to College: A History of the East Side, by Samantha Johnson, 2018
timeline.evidence: when the Kennedy Brothers Company purchased the property to use as a retail outlet for their novelty wood-working business

timeline.detail: Tony Perry bought it in 1981; Lawrence Atkin redesigned the interior and Wendy Coop painted a history mural. Still there as of 2018.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Main to College: A History of the East Side, by Samantha Johnson, 2018
timeline.evidence: this iconic property was purchased by Tony Perry in 1981, who opened the Sweetwaters Restaurant that still occupies the site.

timeline.detail: The Perry Restaurant Group opened Sweetwaters in 1981 in the historic bank building at 120 Church Street. It closed in September 2022 after 41 years so Pascolo could move in.
timeline.source_label: Seven Days, 2026-08-04

timeline.detail: A 1981 mural showed Burlington figures such as Mayor Bernie Sanders, musician Big Joe Burrell and Lois Bodoky, the Church Street hot dog lady. It remains tiled over.
timeline.source_label: Seven Days, 2026-08-04

timeline.detail: Pascolo moved into 120 Church Street from 83 Church in 2022 and ran about three years before returning to 83.
timeline.source_label: Seven Days, 2026-01-23

timeline.detail: Sweetwaters reopened at its original location on Thursday, April 23, 2026 under David Melincoff.

timeline.detail: Neoclassical bank by Harper and West, built by Cashman on the YMCA section; wraps around the McAuliffe Building. A financial and office building since 1931, with retail storefronts as of 2018.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, The City Hall Block - College Street to Main Street, West Side, by Adam King, 2018
timeline.evidence: Since its construction in 1931, the building has been a financial institution and office building, and today includes retail storefronts.

timeline.what: Neo-classical bank in the City Hall Park district
timeline.detail: The state survey form lists the Merchants Bank (#9) of 1931 as an outstanding Neo-classical building in the streetscape looking west from Church Street. HP206 King identifies 123 Church as the 1931 Chittenden County Trust Company building by Harper and West.
timeline.source_label: Vermont Division for Historic Preservation, City Hall Park Historic District survey form (John Page, 2010)
timeline.note: The form does not give street numbers, so the match between survey #9 and 123 Church is not confirmed.

timeline.detail: First structure on the lot: a small one-story building.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Main to College: A History of the East Side, by Samantha Johnson, 2018
timeline.evidence: The 1885 Sanborn map was the first one to show a small, almost square, one-story, composition-roofed building there, occupied by a news dealer.

timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Main to College: A History of the East Side, by Samantha Johnson, 2018
timeline.evidence: From around 1894 to 1912, #124 was a florist shop operated by John Wilson.

timeline.detail: Back to one story by 1912; part of #126 by 1919.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Main to College: A History of the East Side, by Samantha Johnson, 2018
timeline.evidence: by 1919, the property had been absorbed by its southern neighbor, #126.

timeline.detail: Footprint doubled in the 1890s; two stories by 1900.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Main to College: A History of the East Side, by Samantha Johnson, 2018
timeline.evidence: The building was enlarged in the 1890s, doubling the footprint, and by 1900 it was two stories tall

timeline.detail: Wood-framed building divided into barber shop, market and eating saloon.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Main to College: A History of the East Side, by Samantha Johnson, 2018
timeline.evidence: According to the 1869 Sanborn map, there was a one-and-a-half-story, wood-framed commercial building covering these two properties.

timeline.detail: Built on filled ravine land as the temporary post office.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Transitional Blocks: Maple Street to Main Street, east side, by Lynda Howell, 2018
timeline.evidence: It served as post office from 1906 to 1908, and then as a laboratory for the Vermont Department of Health.

timeline.detail: The lab moved to Colchester Avenue in 1919.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Transitional Blocks: Maple Street to Main Street, east side, by Lynda Howell, 2018
timeline.evidence: Since 1919, when the laboratory moved to Colchester Avenue, it has been an apartment building.

timeline.detail: Apartments since 1919.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Transitional Blocks: Maple Street to Main Street, east side, by Lynda Howell, 2018
timeline.evidence: Since 1919, when the laboratory moved to Colchester Avenue, it has been an apartment building.

timeline.detail: The city called 184 Church Street a success story: long vacant, it was under renovation in April 2026 to provide 17 housing units.
A March 1961 fire injured two firemen and left more than thirty people homeless; rebuilt without the third floor or turret tops.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Transitional Blocks: Maple Street to Main Street, east side, by Lynda Howell, 2018
timeline.evidence: In March 1961, a fire attributed to "children playing with matches" gutted the building.

timeline.detail: Built in the late 1890s on filled ravine land, with three floors and two turrets; apartments ever since.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Transitional Blocks: Maple Street to Main Street, east side, by Lynda Howell, 2018
timeline.evidence: 190 Church Street was built in the late 1890s as apartments, and has been so ever since.

timeline.detail: The name D. Blackman appears at the King and Church corner on an 1862 map. The page calls this the oldest structure on the block; build year unknown.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: the name, D. Blackman, was finally put on a map in 1862 in the same corner.

timeline.detail: The house first appears in directories in 1884, addressed to King Street; grocer A.L. Barrows lived there afterward.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: This house did not identify by an address in the city directories until 1884 and was listed as 139 King Street instead of Church Street.

timeline.detail: A produce dealer began living in the home sometime between 1890 and 1892.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: A.L Barrows, a very well-known grocer, began residing in this house until a produce dealer started residing in the home somewhere between 1890 and 1892.

timeline.detail: Hathorne partnered with Van A. Nye selling produce at the corner until moving to a store in 1893.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: This produce dealer, Henry G. Hathorne became business partners with Van A. Nye in 1892 and they started to sell produce together at the corner of King and Church until moving to a store in 1893.

timeline.detail: Hathorne took in teacher boarders in 1895, widening to other low-income workers in 1897.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: Hathorne began to open up his home for boarding in 1895 to teachers and it grew to individuals with other low-income professions in 1897.

timeline.detail: Lived in by a single family from 1903 until 1948.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: The house was lived in by a single family from 1903 until 1948 and then the dwelling became 199 Church Street in 1949.

timeline.detail: A hose was kept on the corner house for an hour during the 1917 fire.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: The house on the corner of King and Church was said to be in danger of the flames so a water hose was kept on the structure for an hour.

timeline.detail: The dwelling became 199 Church Street in 1949.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: The house was lived in by a single family from 1903 until 1948 and then the dwelling became 199 Church Street in 1949.

timeline.detail: The building became a house and business when Peggy Ryan made gowns there.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: The structure became both a house and a business in 1951 when Peggy Ryan started making gowns out of her home until 1960.

timeline.detail: Great Northern Woodworks took over in 1978; as of 2018 it is Great Northern Construction, still in the building. The page's 1970 sentence is garbled.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: Great Northern Woodworks took over the building in 1978 along with other tenants.

timeline.what: Built for New England Tel. & Tel.
timeline.detail: Built as administrative offices for the telephone company.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Transitional Blocks: Maple Street to Main Street, east side, by Lynda Howell, 2018
timeline.evidence: The building that now houses Burlington Telecom was built in 1951 as administrative offices for New England Telegraph & Telephone.

timeline.detail: UVM purchased the building in 1953; after the phone company left in the early 1970s it used it for library storage.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Transitional Blocks: Maple Street to Main Street, east side, by Lynda Howell, 2018
timeline.evidence: the University of Vermont (which had purchased the building in 1953) attempted without success to sell the building

timeline.detail: Sold in 1980 and used as offices since, with tenants including Howard Mental Health, General Electric, and Long Distance North. As of 2018: City HR, Community Justice Center, Burlington Telecom.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Transitional Blocks: Maple Street to Main Street, east side, by Lynda Howell, 2018
timeline.evidence: In 1980, the building finally sold and some of the proceeds were used to build the Library Research Annex on East Avenue.

timeline.detail: Two apartment buildings grouped as one property with seventeen units; both first appear in directories in 1897.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: they both first appear in the city directories in 1897.

timeline.detail: 205 was listed as Mary Riley's boarding house.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: 205 is listed as Mary Riley’s boarding house from 1908 until 1920.

timeline.detail: LaFrance Bowling Alley owner moved in 1930 and died between 1944 and 1946, around when the McAllister photo was taken.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: LaFrance first moved into the building in 1930 and passed away between 1944 and 1946

timeline.detail: The first tenant listed was widow Margaret Kennedy in 1897.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: The first tenant listed at this address was Margaret Kennedy, a widow, in 1897.

timeline.detail: The page says the two-family home was built in 1899, after its first listed tenant.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: 211 Church Street, is a two-family home, built in 1899

timeline.detail: Only one person was listed at a time until 1949.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: Only one person at a time was listed at this location until 1949 when there were two tenants, one being Lucius Jackson.

timeline.detail: An 1893 ad calls Parry's shop at Church and Maple the largest in Burlington; he is listed at 217 the year after 1895 and left in 1904.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: Parry left his shop on Church Street in 1904

timeline.detail: The address first appears in 1895: Joseph Lefebvre, carriage trimmer, and George E. McCannon, carriage painter. The original building no longer exists.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: The first tenant listed is Joseph Lefebvre, a carriage trimmer, who used this address as his shop along with George E. McCannon, a carriage painter.

timeline.detail: Cummings replaced McCannon in 1898 and was gone the following year.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: In 1898, Issac Cummings took George E. McCannon’s spot as carriage painter

timeline.detail: Collins had his shop on the site from 1902 to 1934; its roof caught fire in the 1917 blaze.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: John Collins, a blacksmith arrived in 1902 and had his shop on the site until 1934.

timeline.detail: Joseph and Sam Agel ran a livery.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: the Agel Bros., Joseph and Sam, turned the shop into a livery in 1906 but only stayed until 1907.

timeline.detail: Carriage blacksmiths and painters and a carriage trimmer; Tuttle gone by 1912, Thompson by 1913.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: In 1909, E.P. Tuttle & Sons, carriage blacksmith and painters, had their shop next to John Collins as well as H.F. Thompson, a carriage trimmer.

timeline.detail: Richards took over in 1913 until 1915; the 1917 fire account still calls him the vulcanizer at 217.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: Thompson had left the property and Charles A. Richards, a vulcanizer, had taken over until 1915.

timeline.detail: Carriage manufacturer and blacksmith.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: William A. Robarge, carriage manufacturer and blacksmith, arrived in 1914 and stayed until 1920.

timeline.detail: A mid-modern two-family home built in 1939 after the site was an auto shop and furniture storage; still standing as of 2018.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: The fifth structure on the west block is a mid-modern-style, two-family home built in 1939

timeline.detail: John W. Johnson ran his granite works next to his house at 221, which no longer exists, until retiring in 1932.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: he ran his granite works business next door to his house, at 221 Church Street, which no longer exists.

timeline.detail: A fire damaged the second floor and the building became a focus for rent activists.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Transitional Blocks: Maple Street to Main Street, east side, by Lynda Howell, 2018
timeline.evidence: In 1979, a fire damaged the second floor beyond what the landlord could afford to repair

timeline.detail: The King Street Revitalization Corporation bought it with a federal grant.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Transitional Blocks: Maple Street to Main Street, east side, by Lynda Howell, 2018
timeline.evidence: The King Street Revitalization Corporation purchased the building with the assistance of a federal grant in 1980 and converted it to subsidized housing.

timeline.detail: Probably built around 1890 as a tenement for an absentee landlord; previously numbered 222-228 Church Street.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Transitional Blocks: Maple Street to Main Street, east side, by Lynda Howell, 2018
timeline.evidence: this building was probably built around 1890 "as an income producing tenement for an absentee builder-landlord."

timeline.detail: The six original apartments were divided in the 1940s.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: Transitional Blocks: Maple Street to Main Street, east side, by Lynda Howell, 2018
timeline.evidence: The original six large apartments were divided in the 1940s to make sixteen units

timeline.detail: A three-family Queen Anne home built in 1900; stone cutter John W. Johnson was its first resident and lived there until 1943.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: This address, 223 Church Street, first appears in the city directories in 1900 and John W. Johnson was its first resident.

timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: is a modern commercial building that was built in 1948.

timeline.detail: Formerly a glass blowing studio; as of 2018 home of Soundtoys with the front vacant.
timeline.source_label: UVM HP206, Historic Church Street Blocks, Burlington, Vermont: King Street to Maple Street - West Side, by Kristi Bodine, 2018
timeline.evidence: This structure was home to a glass blowing studio and is now the home of Soundtoys although, the front of the building is vacant.
